## TL;DR

Addressed Review 10's partial-replay ordering issue. Replayed bookkeeping commits now receive a narrowly scoped internal allowance, while any new commit arriving during a pending replay continues through the normal gate hook and is appended behind the remaining queue. Added a regression that acquires a production check-gate lock, queues writes through `commitFiles`, lets the first queued commit land, forces the second replay to fail through Git's pre-commit hook, then verifies a third write is deferred and all three commits replay in order after recovery.

## Work and rationale

The previous queue regression constructed the partial-replay sequence through the enqueue helper. That checked snapshot bookkeeping but did not prove that a new RepoOS write arriving after a failed flush would pass through the production commit hook. The new test exercises the full route: the installed check-gate hook receives writes through `commitFiles`, holder release flushes the queue, an actual Git hook rejects the second replay, and stale-lock recovery retries after the Git hook is removed.

The failure exposed an overly broad internal replay bypass. The flush path marked the entire replay window as internal, so the commit hook treated any write during that window as allowed. The hook now recognizes only the exact replay commit currently being applied, matching its worktree, message, and absolute paths. The internal Git-command allowance is scoped to that synchronous `commitFiles` call. A new bookkeeping commit therefore encounters the pending lock and is queued behind entries that remain. Queue snapshots continue to record the latest on-disk contents, while replay progress is persisted after each successful commit; recovery can resume from the committed entry and apply later snapshots in order.

The source-write limitation remains intentional and documented. RepoOS refuses to start a new managed engineer turn while a check lock is active, and committed source drift is inspected at the commit level after the check. An already-running engineer can still make direct filesystem edits; those edits are detected after the fact through drift checking and can invalidate the result. The implementation does not claim to block arbitrary filesystem writes.

No `repoos.toml` changes or runtime dependencies were introduced. The fix is confined to the lock/replay path and its regression test.

## Approaches tried

I first extended the existing helper-level replay test with the exact sequence from the review: first entry committed, second entry fails, and a third write arrives. To make the test representative of production behavior, I replaced simulated failure with a temporary Git pre-commit hook and routed all writes through `commitFiles` after installing the production gate hook. The first iteration configured the hook in the wrong worktree repository, so it did not run; correcting its scope confirmed the test exercises the task worktree. A second iteration tried to inspect `COMMIT_EDITMSG` in `pre-commit`, but Git has not prepared that file at that hook stage. The final hook fails based on the replayed task-file snapshot, so it deterministically rejects only the second entry.

I then narrowed the replay bypass from the full flush duration to the specific queued commit. The focused bookkeeping test file passes with the new production-path regression, including assertions that the pending queue remains protected, the later write does not move HEAD around the failed entry, and recovery produces the expected commit order and final contents.

## Challenges and blockers

An earlier handoff check was still running when Review 10 arrived. I kept its tree stable until it had begun, then applied the requested fix and regression; its result cannot validate this updated tree, so a fresh `repoos check --changed main` is required before handoff. During regression development, the temporary failure hook initially did not trigger because its Git configuration was applied to the board repository rather than the task worktree. I corrected the test setup and verified the expected partial replay and recovery behavior through the production commit path.

## Key learnings

A replay-wide “internal” flag can accidentally weaken the very queue fence that replay is meant to preserve. Internal permission should identify the one commit being replayed, while other bookkeeping writes must continue to enter the durable queue. Tests for crash recovery should include writes arriving after partial progress through the same production entry point used by normal server bookkeeping, not only direct queue-helper calls. Source edits by an already-running engineer remain a post-write detection case; documentation and reports should describe that limitation precisely.
